hero.heading: Quantum-Inspired Optimization for Deadlock-Aware Scheduling
hero.description: We compare three approaches on identical generated inputs: the classical Banker's Algorithm, a Quantum-Inspired Evolutionary Algorithm (QEA), and a Banker + QEA hybrid. Every result on this site comes from measured, reproducible Java benchmarks — not from assumptions.

approaches.title: Banker's Algorithm
approaches.subtitle: Classical Safety Baseline
approaches.description: Silberschatz's safety algorithm checks whether a resource-allocation state can lead every process to completion without deadlock. Deterministic and polynomial-time O(n²m). Our baseline.

approaches.title: QEA Alone
approaches.subtitle: Quantum-Inspired Evolutionary
approaches.description: Uses a population of Q-bit individuals (angle representation) to search for low-fitness execution orders. Safety is a soft penalty, not a hard constraint. Stochastic — results vary by seed.

approaches.title: Banker + QEA Hybrid
approaches.subtitle: Safety-Constrained Search
approaches.description: Banker's Algorithm acts as a hard gate inside the fitness function. Unsafe candidates receive a fitness of MAX_VALUE/2, so QEA only optimises among provably safe schedules.

disclaimer.heading: What We Are NOT Claiming
disclaimer.intro: Intellectual honesty is a first-class project requirement. These points are printed here so they appear in every demo, viva and report review.

items.title: QEA is not a quantum computer algorithm
items.body: Quantum-Inspired Evolutionary Algorithms (QIEAs) use the mathematical formalism of qubits — superposition and rotation — as a metaphor for probabilistic search. All computation runs on a classical JVM. No quantum hardware is involved or claimed.

items.title: No quantum speedup is claimed
items.body: Our benchmark shows QEA is 4–120× slower than Banker's Algorithm depending on problem size. This is expected and honest. The QEA's potential value lies in solution quality on hard multi-objective problems, not raw speed.

items.title: QEA does not replace Banker's Algorithm
items.body: Banker's Algorithm gives a definitive safety verdict in O(n²m). QEA searches for good execution orders within the feasible space. They answer different questions. The hybrid combines both.

items.title: A cycle in the RAG does not prove deadlock with multi-instance resources
items.body: Cycle detection via DFS is sufficient for single-instance resources. For multi-instance resources, a cycle is necessary but not sufficient for deadlock — Banker's Algorithm is required for a definitive verdict. Our Silberschatz test (T8 in Step 4) demonstrates this explicitly.

items.title: Results are measured, never assumed
items.body: Every number in the results section comes from the actual Java benchmark (390 runs). No result is interpolated, averaged-away, or cherry-picked. The fairness panel shows cases where Banker is faster and where QEA brings no improvement.

coffman.heading: Deadlock & the Four Coffman Conditions
coffman.intro: A deadlock occurs when a set of processes is permanently blocked, each waiting for a resource held by another. All four conditions must hold simultaneously.

conditions.name: Mutual Exclusion
conditions.description: At least one resource must be held in a non-shareable mode — only one process can use it at a time.

conditions.name: Hold and Wait
conditions.description: A process holding at least one resource is waiting to acquire additional resources held by other processes.

conditions.name: No Preemption
conditions.description: Resources cannot be forcibly taken from a process; they must be released voluntarily.

conditions.name: Circular Wait
conditions.description: A set of processes P₁,P₂,...,Pₙ exists such that P₁ waits for P₂, P₂ waits for P₃, ..., Pₙ waits for P₁.

items.name: Available[m]
items.description: Vector of currently free instances of each resource type.

items.name: Maximum[n][m]
items.description: Maximum demand of each process for each resource type.

items.name: Allocation[n][m]
items.description: Currently allocated instances of each resource type to each process.

items.name: Need[n][m]
items.description: Remaining need = Maximum − Allocation. Must be ≥ 0.

items.name: Work[m]
items.description: Working copy of Available, updated as processes are simulated to finish.

items.name: Finish[n]
items.description: Boolean array: Finish[i] = true once process i can complete in the simulation.

comparisonTable.heading: Which Question Does Each Method Answer?

Does a safe sequence exist?
rows.answer_safe: Safe sequence found → state is safe
rows.answer_unsafe: No safe sequence → state is unsafe (definitive)

rows.question: Which execution order minimises fitness?
rows.answer_unsafe: Best schedule is still penalised by deadlock weight

fitness.heading: Fitness Function
fitness.note: Lower is better. DeadlockPenalty = 1 if any process is permanently blocked, 0 otherwise. In Hybrid mode, unsafe states receive Double.MAX_VALUE/2 and are never selected.

experimentalDesign.heading: Experimental Design & Fairness
principles: One SystemState generated per size, per seed — all three algorithms receive deepCopy() of the same state
Banker: 5 repetitions (deterministic; repeated only for timing statistics)
QEA and Hybrid: 30 repetitions each (stochastic; sequential seeds 1000..1029)
All runs logged — no cherry-picking; results.csv contains every single repetition
Same hardware and JVM for all measurements
Fairness flags are automatically computed and displayed
